channel.title: The Coin Wire
channel.description: Crypto news on Bitcoin, Ethereum, DeFi, stablecoins, exchanges, regulation and protocol upgrades: what changed, and what comes next.

item.title: A bridge change does not move a rollup treasury’s assets
item.description: A bridge update does not move treasury balances by itself. Map token contracts, compare withdrawal and liquidity routes, then migrate in verified stages.

item.title: Bitcoin and EVM swaps need different routes
item.description: Bitcoin transfers spend UTXOs and pay by transaction size; EVM swaps execute contracts and need gas, so the right route depends on where the asset must end up.

item.title: Four checks before swapping a rebasing token
item.description: Before signing a rebasing-token swap, check the asset, balance model, route support and execution limits; each can change what arrives and how much you keep.

item.title: A Practical Method for Settling Cross-Chain Crypto Invoices
item.description: Settle a cross-chain crypto invoice by fixing its value, naming the destination chain and agreeing who bears conversion, transfer and timing risk upfront.

item.title: Why bridged stablecoins can trade below their local peg
item.description: Bridged stablecoins can slip below a dollar when redemption routes, liquidity or trust differ from the issuer-backed token, even if both share a ticker.

item.title: A crypto swap resets the cost basis of both sides
item.description: A crypto swap can realize a gain or loss and start a new basis for the asset received, so each trade needs its own value, fee and lot records.

item.title: Judge keeps Gemini’s $5 million CFTC order in force
item.description: A New York judge left Gemini’s $5 million CFTC consent order intact, rejecting both sides’ effort to lift its injunction after the agency disavowed the case.

item.title: Why Wallets Switch Networks Before a Bridge Signature
item.description: A wallet switches to a bridge’s required chain to prepare the right signing context; the network prompt alone does not approve or move funds.

item.title: Why Bridge Minimums Matter in Small Treasury Rebalances
item.description: Bridge minimums can make a small treasury move uneconomic or unavailable; learn what sets the floor, how it differs from slippage, and when to split or wait.

item.title: Moving Stablecoin Savings Into Bitcoin Means Choosing What to Keep Liquid
item.description: Moving stablecoins into bitcoin means choosing a conversion route, deciding how much liquidity to keep, and matching custody to your time horizon and risk.

item.title: Cross-chain swap quotes depend on the route, not just the rate
item.description: Compare cross-chain swap quotes by matching the route and measuring destination value after fees, slippage, gas, execution risk and expiry.

item.title: When a Dapp Rejects a Bridged Token, Check the Chain First
item.description: A rejected token often remains on the destination chain; trace the bridge state first, then decide whether to import, claim, swap or return it safely.

item.title: Why Small Cross-Chain Swaps Cost More Proportionally
item.description: A small cross-chain swap carries many of the same transaction steps as a large one, so gas, bridge charges and extra execution weigh more against its value.

item.title: Convert Yield Tokens Before Bridging: What to Check
item.description: Converting a yield token to a bridge-supported asset can simplify a transfer, but fees, lost yield and destination liquidity determine whether it is worth doing.

item.title: How to Diagnose Direct and Multi-Hop Mantle Routes
item.description: Trace a Mantle route by separating its source transaction, bridge message and destination action; each stage points to a different cause when funds stall.

item.title: Two explorers show what a bridge quote leaves out
item.description: A bridge quote is an estimate; two chain explorers show the source fee actually paid on-chain and whether a separate destination transaction completed.

item.title: Why Wallet Bridge Transfers Take Longer Than a Swap
item.description: Bridge transfers take longer because the source chain must confirm a transaction and the destination chain must complete another; wallets often wait for both.

item.title: A confirmation is not the same as cross-chain finality
item.description: Confirmations show that a transaction is gaining support; finality sets a stronger settlement point, and cross-chain swaps must account for both chains and the route between them.

item.title: Moving USDC Between Chains: Choose the Route, Not Just the Fee
item.description: The cheapest quote may leave you with a different USDC version or less on arrival. Compare route mechanics, finality, liquidity and destination support before swapping.

item.title: Why a confirmed crypto transfer can still be stuck
item.description: A source-chain confirmation does not guarantee arrival: bridge relayers, proofs, liquidity and destination execution each add separate steps and failure modes.
